drills.name: Chūdan-no-kamae
drills.desc: The central guard: shinai tip aimed at the opponent's throat, left fist a fist's width from the navel, weight slightly forward. Everything attacks and defends from here, so the posture must stay tall and relaxed with the shoulders down for entire keiko sessions.
mistakes: Shoulders creeping up toward the ears, freezing every strike that follows.
The shinai tip drifting off the centerline and surrendering the throat line.
Leaning back with the weight on the heels.

drills.name: Tenouchi
drills.desc: The wringing squeeze of both little and ring fingers at the exact moment of impact, which stops the shinai crisply and gives the strike its snap. Between strikes the grip is soft like holding an egg — tenouchi is a pulse, not a clench.
mistakes: Gripping hard the whole time, so the strike lands dead with no snap.
Squeezing with thumb and index instead of the last two fingers.

drills.name: Okuri-ashi
drills.desc: The gliding step of kendo: right foot slides forward, left foot instantly draws up behind, heels barely brushing the floor, left heel always slightly raised. Speed in kendo is really the left leg — it is loaded like a spring and drives every advance.
mistakes: Left heel dropping flat, discharging the spring.
Crossing or stepping the feet past each other instead of sliding.
Bouncing tall with each step rather than gliding level.

drills.name: Fumikomi
drills.desc: The explosive stamp of the right foot that lands in the same instant as the strike, expressing ki-ken-tai-ichi — spirit, sword and body as one. The lunge is driven entirely by the left leg; the stamp is flat-footed and forward, followed immediately by the left foot snapping up.
mistakes: Stamping down hard on the heel — an injury generator with no forward drive.
Foot landing before or after the strike instead of together with it.
Left foot dragging behind after the stamp, killing follow-through.

drills.name: Jōge-buri
drills.desc: The largest practice swing: shinai raised until it nearly touches the back, then cut down to knee height in one relaxed arc. It teaches the full cutting path and loosens the shoulders — the swing should feel like the arms are thrown, not pushed.
mistakes: Bending the elbows sharply at the top instead of keeping a wide arc.
Cutting with tense shoulders so the swing is muscled rather than whipped.

drills.name: Shōmen-suburi
drills.desc: Repeated cuts to head height, raising the shinai above the head and snapping it down to stop level at men, coordinated with a step. The left hand powers and steers the cut down the centerline while the right only guides — hundreds of correct repetitions build the kendo cut.
mistakes: Pushing the cut with the right hand so the tip drifts off center.
Stopping the cut with stiff arms instead of tenouchi snap.

drills.name: Haya-suburi
drills.desc: Continuous fast suburi with a small forward-back jump on every swing — the classic kendo conditioning drill. It welds the swing to the footwork under fatigue: the goal is keeping the cut large and the posture tall when the legs are burning.
mistakes: Swings shrinking to tired little chops as the set goes on.
Jumping high instead of skimming forward and back.
Posture folding forward at the hips under fatigue.

drills.name: Men-uchi
drills.desc: The fundamental strike: launch from chūdan with the left leg, cut straight down the centerline to the top of the men, stamp landing with the blow. A valid men is posture, cut, stamp and kiai in one instant — power comes from the body arriving, not the arms swinging harder.
mistakes: Leaning the head and shoulders forward to reach instead of driving the body in.
Cutting men while the feet are still — hand and foot must land together.

drills.name: Kote-uchi
drills.desc: A small, sharp cut to the opponent's right wrist, raising the shinai just enough to clear their tip before snapping down. It is the most compact strike in kendo — nearly all wrist and tenouchi, launched with a short, sudden fumikomi.
mistakes: Raising the shinai as high as for men, telegraphing the small strike.
Hitting flat across the kote instead of cutting down through it.

drills.name: Dō-uchi
drills.desc: A diagonal cut to the right side of the opponent's dō, usually as they raise their arms to attack men. The blade angles through with a turn of the wrists and a twist of the trunk, followed by passing through to the opponent's side — the only routinely diagonal cut in kendo.
mistakes: Slapping the dō flat because the wrists never turn the blade edge-on.
Stopping in front of the opponent after the cut instead of passing through.

drills.name: Kote-men
drills.desc: The classic renzoku-waza: a fast kote that draws the block, chained instantly into men as the opponent reacts. It demands two fumikomi in rapid succession — the left foot must recover under the body between strikes or the men arrives powerless.
mistakes: Throwing a fake kote with no threat — the opponent never reacts.
The left foot failing to snap up between strikes, leaving the men flat-footed.

drills.name: Kirikaeshi
drills.desc: The cornerstone paired drill: shōmen, then a flowing series of alternating left-right men cuts advancing and retreating, repeated with full spirit in one breath. It forges swing mechanics, distance, breathing and endurance at once — every kendo practice begins and ends with it.
mistakes: Cutting straight down on the diagonal sayu-men instead of at 45 degrees.
Holding the breath and fading halfway instead of riding one long kiai.
Feet stopping while the arms keep swinging — strikes disconnect from steps.

drills.name: Uchikomi-geiko
drills.desc: The motodachi opens a target — men, kote, dō — and the trainee strikes it immediately with full commitment and follow-through. It trains instant recognition and total commitment: see the opening, launch, strike, pass through, turn ready again.
mistakes: Hesitating a beat after the opening appears — the moment is already gone.
Decelerating before impact instead of striking through the target.

drills.name: Kakari-geiko
drills.desc: Short, furious rounds of non-stop attacking against a receiving partner — no defense, no pause, technique after technique until time is called. It burns out hesitation and builds the anaerobic engine that lets clean cuts survive the final seconds of a match.
mistakes: Pacing yourself — kakari-geiko only works at maximum output.
Form collapsing into wild slaps instead of full, correct cuts under fatigue.

drills.name: Seme & tobikomi-men
drills.alt: Pressuring in, then leaping head strike
drills.desc: Creating the opening yourself: a half-step of seme that pressures the opponent's center and forces a flinch, then an explosive leaping men into the gap. The strike covers maximum distance from a stolen inch — the deepest expression of the loaded left leg and unbroken posture.
mistakes: Stepping in without threatening the center — seme with no pressure is just standing closer.
Launching off the front leg instead of the loaded left leg.
Breaking posture forward to reach, so the strike lands weak and short.
